Otherwise it looks the rows up through `RowManager` and returns those (each once) whose item the user cannot see, judged through the item's type with the user's real permissions (no security override); rows that do not exist are included (and logged). A row whose item is a loop marker is judged by the item of the row the marker refers to.

Negative (temporary) row IDs passed to `getInvisibleRows`: with Java assertions enabled (as the tests run) the call throws `AssertionError`; with them disabled the negative IDs are dropped and only the others are checked (all negative gives an empty set).

Results of `getInvisibleRows` are cached per user: a row already checked for that user is answered from the cache without asking the item types again. When `ItemTracker` reports changed items, the cached results for the rows that show those items (found with `RowManager.findRows`) are dropped on that user's next call; a full update from the tracker drops the user's whole cache. All cached data is also dropped on the first call made more than 5 minutes after the last full clear.

`collectInvisibleIssues(issues, user, override, collector)` adds each given issue ID at most once, in ascending order, when a Jira index search for `id in (...)` run as the user (with the security-override flag as given) does not return it; deleted or unknown issues are therefore reported. The search runs in chunks of Jira's maximum clause count (or `structure.matchIssuesSorted.chunkSize` when positive). If the search fails, all issues being checked are reported, and if the index is unusable (reindex in progress or inconsistent) all are reported too.

Results of `collectInvisibleIssues` are cached per user key (anonymous under an empty key); all calls with the security override share one cache regardless of user. An issue's cached result is dropped when `ItemTracker` reports a change to that issue. Results that came from a failed search (all reported as invisible) are cached like any other until the issue changes or the cache is cleared (as the original does).

`getInvisibleItems(items, user)` groups the items by item type. All items of a type that is not available are invisible. For a type implementing `BulkAccessCheckingItemType` its `filterInaccessible` is called once with the group (override false); for other types each item is invisible when `accessItem` returns null or `isVisible(item, user)` is false. If the check of a type throws an `Exception` or `LinkageError`, all items of that type are invisible. This method keeps no cache: every call asks the item types.

`collectInvisibleRows(forest, user, collector)` takes each row's item from the `ItemForest` itself (so temporary rows work), resolving a loop-marker item through `RowManager.getRow` of the referenced row (a missing referenced row makes the call fail with `MissingRowException`), judges the items as `getInvisibleItems` does without security override, and adds the invisible rows in forest order. Its results are not cached.

`clear()` drops all cached data and restarts the 5-minute expiry period. `clear(key)` drops only that user's row and issue results computed without security override; null does nothing, and the anonymous user's data is kept under the empty key, so only `clear("")` or a full clear removes it; the shared security-override issue cache is removed only by a full clear or expiry. As a caching component, `clearCaches()` drops everything without restarting the expiry period and `clearUserCaches(user)` equals `clear(user.getKey())`.
When `StructureConfiguration.isEnabledForAllProjects()` is true, `collectOutOfScopeIssues` adds nothing and does no index search.

Otherwise the allowed projects are `StructureConfiguration.getPickedProjectIds()`. The project ID of each given issue is read from the Jira index field `projid` with security overridden (no permission check), and an issue is added when that project is not among the picked ones (a value that is not a number counts as 0). Issues not found in the index are not added. Each issue ID is added at most once, in ascending order; an empty picked list makes every indexed issue out of scope.

The project configuration is read on first use and kept until the cache is cleared (`clearCaches()`, or automatically on the first call more than 5 minutes after the last full clear), so a configuration change is not seen before that. Per-issue results are cached as well and dropped for an issue when `ItemTracker` reports it changed (for example moved to another project).

If the index search fails with a `SearchException`, all issues being checked are reported as out of scope. If the index is unusable (full reindex running or inconsistent), nothing is reported for them. Either outcome is cached until the issue changes or the cache is cleared (as the original does).
`clearUserCaches(user)` does nothing; `clearCaches()` drops the cached configuration and all results.
`collectSubTaskIssues` adds nothing and does no search when Jira's `SubTaskManager.isSubTasksEnabled()` is false or `ConstantsManager.getSubTaskIssueTypeObjects()` is empty.

Otherwise the issue type of each given issue is read from the Jira index field `type` with security overridden, and the issue is added when that type is one of the sub-task issue types (type IDs that are not numbers never match). Issues not found in the index are not added; each issue ID is added at most once, in ascending order.

The set of sub-task types (and whether sub-tasks are enabled) is read on first use and kept until the cache is cleared (`clearCaches()`, or on the first call more than 5 minutes after the last full clear). Per-issue answers are cached too and dropped for an issue when `ItemTracker` reports it changed.

If the index search fails with a `SearchException`, all issues being checked are reported as sub-tasks; if the index is unusable, none are. Either outcome is cached until the issue changes or the cache is cleared (as the original does). `clearUserCaches(user)` does nothing.

`parse(null)` throws `NullPointerException`. A successful `parse(text)` returns a new query each call whose `getQueryString()` and `toString()` both return `text` unchanged. Parsing only checks syntax and the names of registered constraints: no issue, JQL field or permission is checked (that happens in `validate` and before execution).

Every syntax error throws `StructureException` with error code 6005 (category INVALID_INPUT; a plugin code that is not in `StructureErrors`). Its localized message quotes the text up to and including the error position, at most the last 40 characters, between single quotes, with `...` where text was cut off before or after, followed by the line and column. Examples that fail: the empty string or only whitespace, `root xyz`, `root)`, `(root`, `child root`, `child in`, `PROJ-1 PROJ-2`.

Keywords are matched without regard to case, and each spelling with underscores also has a camelCase form: `prev_sibling`, `prevSibling`, `PREVSIBLING` and `Prev_Sibling` are the same keyword. A keyword must end at whitespace, the end, or a character that cannot continue a word (`orx` is not `or`). Synonyms: `empty`/`null`; `leaf`/`leaves`; `root`/`roots`; `issue`/`issues`; `child`/`children`/`sub_issue`/`sub_issues`; singular and plural of parent, descendant, ancestor and sibling; `preceding_sibling`/`prev_sibling`/`previous_sibling` (and plurals); `following_sibling`/ `next_sibling` (and plurals).

`or`/`||`/`|`, `and`/`&&`/`&` and `not`/`!` combine clauses; `not` binds tightest, then `and`, then `or`, and repeated `not` is allowed (`not not leaf` equals `leaf`). Parentheses group. `A or B and C` selects rows matching A, or matching both B and C.

On a forest, `empty`/`null` match no rows; `leaf` matches rows without children; `root` matches top-level rows; `[]` (JQL with no condition) matches every row whose item is an issue the current user can see.

A comma-separated list of issue keys and numeric IDs (e.g. `PROJ-1, proj-2, 10001`) matches the rows whose item is one of those issues. A numeric ID matches its issue's rows directly. A key is looked up with Jira's `IssueManager.getIssueByKeyIgnoreCase` and matches only if the current user has `BROWSE_PROJECTS` on the issue (unless security is overridden); keys or IDs of issues not present in the forest simply match nothing. A key or ID followed directly by a letter or digit (e.g. `10001abc`, `PROJ-1x`) is a syntax error; a JQL clause inside the list is a syntax error.

`[ ... ]` embeds Jira JQL, parsed with Jira's `JqlQueryParser`; the closing bracket is found while skipping quoted strings (backslash escapes inside them) and custom-field references like `cf[10010]`. An ORDER BY part is dropped. The clause matches rows whose item is an issue matched by that JQL as the current user (security override respected); rows of other item types never match. A JQL parse error is reported as a syntax error (code 6005) carrying Jira's localized JQL message; a missing `]` is a syntax error of its own.

For a relation R and clause C: `R in C`, `R = C` and `R is C` match rows that have at least one R-relative matching C (`child in C`: rows with a child matching C; `ancestor in C`: rows below a row matching C); `R of C` matches the R-relatives of rows matching C (`child of C`: children of matching rows); `R not in C`, `R != C` and `R is not C` match the rows that `R in C` does not. `self` relates a row to itself; `issue` relates an issue row to itself only. C after an operator is a single clause (possibly negated or itself relational); `and`/`or` need parentheses.

With `empty` as the clause: `R in empty` and `R is empty` match rows that have no R-relative (`child is empty` equals `leaf`); `R not in empty` matches rows that have at least one; `R of empty` matches rows that are not an R-relative of any row (`child of empty` equals `root`).

`prev_sibling` relates a row to every earlier row with the same parent (not only the adjacent one; top-level rows are siblings of each other), `next_sibling` to every later one, and `sibling` to both. So `prev_sibling of C` matches all earlier siblings of each row matching C.

Combined relation names `issue_or_R`, `issues_or_R`, `R_or_issue`, `R_or_issues`, `self_or_R` and `R_or_self` exist for R = child, parent, descendant, ancestor and the three sibling relations (all spellings), and mean the union of the two relations (`self_or_child in C` = rows matching C or having a child matching C). Relations can also be joined explicitly before one operator: `self or child in C` means the same; the relation after `or` must be a relation, else it is a syntax error.

A registered constraint name (case-insensitive; an unregistered name is a syntax error) is used as `name(a, b)`, `name()` (no arguments), `name arg` (one argument running to the next whitespace) or bare `name` when the next token is `and`, `or`, `)` (inside parentheses) or the end. An unquoted argument in parentheses runs to the next `,` or `)` and is trimmed. Quoted arguments use `"..."` or `'...'`; inside, a backslash before `"`, `'` or `\` stands for that character and any other backslash is kept. Syntax errors: an empty argument (`name(a,)`, `name(,a)`), a missing `)`, an unclosed quote.

In the `name arg` form the argument runs up to whitespace only, so `(folder Foo)` passes `Foo)` as the argument and then fails with a syntax error for the missing `)`, while `(folder Foo )` works (as the original does).

A query object remembers the evaluation context of its last execution, including the user and the security override it was created for, and reuses it whenever it is executed again on the same `Forest` instance. So executing the same query object on the same forest instance as a different user evaluates JQL and issue keys for the first user, once the new user passes validation (as the original does). A different forest instance gets a fresh context.
When a named constraint throws during execution (from `filter` or from its sequence), the error is logged and that constraint matches no further rows; the query does not fail.

Each `builder()` call returns the first step of a new, independent builder; finishing it with `end()` gives a query whose `getQueryString()` is null. Built queries are validated and executed exactly like parsed ones (same semantics for every constraint and relation).

In a builder, constraints joined through `and` form one group and `or` starts a new group; the result is the union of the groups, so `a.and.b.or.c` means (a and b) or c. `sub()` ... `endsub()` makes one parenthesized constraint. `not()` negates only the next constraint, and `not().not()` cancels out.

`issueKey(s)`, `issueId(s)` and `issues(keys, ids)` copy their arguments when called (changing the list later has no effect); null key or ID collections count as empty, and a list with no keys and no IDs matches nothing.

`query(q)` inserts the logic of a query made by this plugin (parsed or built) as one constraint; a query of any other `StructureQuery` implementation, or null, is ignored with a warning and the builder is returned unchanged (so `query(foreign).end()` alone matches nothing).

`constraint(name, args...)` with a null argument throws `NullPointerException`. At validation the name is looked up as a prefix among the registered constraint names (case-insensitive) and the first match validates the arguments, so an abbreviation such as `fol` passes validation through `folder`; at execution only an exact (case-insensitive) name matches, and an unknown or abbreviated name matches no rows (as the original does). A name that matches nothing at all gives a validation error.
`.or()` on a relation step joins relations before the operator: `self.or().child.in.C` matches rows that match C or have a child matching C, like the text `self or child in C`.

`toString()` of a built query is generated text: `empty()` gives `EMPTY`; negation is a leading `!` (with parentheses around a compound clause), so `all()` gives `!EMPTY`; an issue list gives the IDs then the keys in parentheses separated by commas, e.g. `(10001,PROJ-1)`; JQL gives `[` + Jira's `JqlStringSupport.generateJqlString` + `]` (`[]` for none); a constraint gives `name("a","b")` with every argument in double quotes and nothing escaped; or-groups are joined by ` || ` and and-groups by ` && `; relational clauses are written in `of` form with lower-case relation names (`child in C` is written `parent of C`) and joined relations with `|`, which the parser does not read back as one relation.

A built query equals (and has the same hash code as) a parsed or built query with the same logic after simplification, whatever the text: for example `child.in.issueKey("A-1")` equals `parse("child in A-1")` and `parse("parent of A-1")`, and a doubly negated constraint equals the constraint itself.

The component decides once, when it is created, whether Jira runs as a cluster: it asks Jira for its com.atlassian.jira.cluster.ClusterInfo component and treats Jira as Data Center only when that component exists and isClustered() is true (the answer is computed once per plugin lifetime). On Data Center, the shared caches (expiring and non-expiring) and the named lockers it hands out are cluster-aware (backed by Jira's com.atlassian.cache.CacheManager and com.atlassian.beehive.ClusterLockService); on a single server they are purely in-memory on this node and Jira's cache manager and cluster lock service are never used. Caches requested explicitly as node-local are always in-memory on this node, in both modes.

On Data Center, a shared cache requested under name N is registered with Jira's CacheManager.getCache under the name "com.almworks.structure." + N, with a loader that stores only a marker (Boolean.TRUE) per key; the cached values themselves are kept in memory on each node. The cache settings map to Jira's com.atlassian.cache.CacheSettingsBuilder as follows: an expire-after-access timeout is applied only when its time unit is set and the timeout is positive, likewise expire-after-write, and maxEntries is set only when the maximum size is positive; with no settings (a non-expiring cache) nothing is set. The same expiry and size settings also apply to the node's own value storage.

On Data Center, reading key K from a shared cache returns the value held in this node's memory only while Jira's cluster cache still contains K; if Jira's cache does not contain K (because it was invalidated on any node, expired or evicted) or this node holds no value, the node drops its own copy, asks Jira's cache for K (which puts the marker back) and computes the value again with the cache's loader. Invalidating K removes K from Jira's cluster cache (so every node recomputes on its next read); invalidating all calls removeAll() on it; 'contains K' and the key list are answered from Jira's cluster cache. If Jira's cache throws com.atlassian.cache.CacheException while putting the marker back, a warning is logged and the value is still computed and returned.

On Data Center, asking twice for a shared cache with the same name returns the same cache object as long as the first one is still referenced by someone (it is held only weakly); the loader and settings of the second request are then ignored. On a single server, and for node-local caches in either mode, every request creates a new, independent cache, even for a name already used.

On Data Center, the node-side part of a shared cache is created on its first use, not when the cache is requested. If creating it fails with a runtime exception or linkage error, a read, a 'contains' check or a key listing throws StructureRuntimeException wrapping the failure, while invalidate and invalidate-all log an error and do nothing; the creation is attempted again on the next use.

A node-local cache (and, on a single server, every shared cache) is an in-memory com.google.common.cache cache built from its settings: expire-after-access and expire-after-write are applied only when the time unit is set and the timeout is positive, a maximum size only when positive, soft values and a concurrency level when requested. A removal listener given in the settings is told the key, the value (null when the entry removed was an invalidated placeholder) and the Guava com.google.common.cache.RemovalCause of every removal. Shared caches requested as non-expiring have no expiry and no size limit. On a single server, requesting a shared expiring cache with no settings object (null) fails with NullPointerException (as the original does).

In a node-local cache, invalidating key K does not delete the entry but replaces its value with an 'invalidated' placeholder: afterwards 'contains K' is false and the next read of K computes the value again with the loader, but the key list still includes K until the entry is evicted or the whole cache is invalidated (as the original does). Invalidate-all empties the cache completely: it waits for a cache-wide lock (taken exclusively, while individual loads hold it shared) and, if that lock cannot be obtained within the lock timeout, logs an 'INCONSISTENCY WARNING' and empties the cache without it. The key list is a snapshot copy that cannot be modified.

When a cache's loader fails, the read fails: a runtime exception thrown by the loader reaches the caller as StructureRuntimeException (wrapping it); a checked exception reaches the caller as a checked 'load failed' exception whose cause is the loader's exception; an InterruptedException from the loader re-sets the thread's interrupt flag and is reported as StructureRuntimeException. A failed load caches nothing, so the next read calls the loader again. The loader must not return null: in node-local caches a null result fails the read with StructureRuntimeException, and in cluster caches with Guava's unchecked 'invalid cache load' exception.

Every cache handed out guards against an invalidation racing with a load, so a value computed before an invalidation is never kept after it: a miss on key K is resolved while holding a per-key lock (one per key, locks for up to 1000 keys are remembered; dark feature com.almworks.jira.structure.cache.locksCacheMaxSize), and if the freshly stored entry has been invalidated again in the meantime the load is retried, up to 5 attempts in total (com.almworks.jira.structure.cache.loadAttempts), pausing 0, 100, 200, 400, 800 ms ... after the successive failed attempts (doubling from com.almworks.jira.structure.cache.repeatedLoadAttemptMinDelay, default 100). If all attempts fail, a warning is logged and the value is computed directly with the loader and returned without being cached. If the per-key lock cannot be taken within 65000 ms (com.almworks.jira.structure.cache.lockTimeoutMs) the value is likewise computed directly and returned uncached. The dark features are read through DarkFeatures when the component is created.

Invalidating one key or all keys of any cache handed out never throws: an exception or linkage error raised while invalidating (for example by Jira's cluster cache) is logged as a warning and swallowed.

The expiry presets the plugin's components use when they request expiring caches are: fast-expiring 60 s, moderately expiring 600 s and slowly expiring 3600 s after last access, each overridable per cache by a DarkFeatures long property named by the requesting component. A JVM system property structure.cache.expiration-override (seconds, decoded as Long.getLong does) replaces every such expire-after-access timeout of every cache, taking precedence over the per-cache property; likewise structure.cache.expiration-after-write-override for presets that expire after write. A value of 0 or less means no expiry.

On Data Center, a named locker N runs a piece of code while holding the Jira cluster lock obtained from ClusterLockService.getLockForName("com.almworks.structure.." + N + "." + id) (note the double dot; id is the lock target's String.valueOf, so a null id gives "null"). A timeout of 0 means the default 65000 ms; a negative timeout means a single immediate tryLock(); otherwise tryLock waits up to the timeout. The lock is released when the code finishes, also when it throws, and the code's exceptions propagate unchanged. If the lock is not obtained in time, a StructureException with error StructureErrors.LOCK_FAILED is thrown and the code is not run; if the waiting thread is interrupted, the same error is thrown (with the InterruptedException as cause) and the thread's interrupt flag is set again. The lock-cache size requested is ignored in this mode.

On a single server, a named locker is an in-memory, per-node lock table: asking twice for the same name returns the same locker (the first request's size wins), keeping per-target reentrant locks for at least 10 and at most max(requested size, 10) idle targets (locks in use are never dropped). Code run for one target excludes other threads running code for the same target (a null target is a valid target of its own) but not for other targets, and the same thread may re-enter. A timeout of 0 means 65000 ms, a positive timeout below 1000 ms is raised to 1000 ms, and a negative timeout means 'only if free right now'. When the lock is not obtained in time, a StructureException with error StructureErrors.LOCK_FAILED is thrown and the code is not run; an interrupted wait gives the same error and re-sets the interrupt flag. The code's own exceptions propagate unchanged and the lock is always released.

The component decides whether the plugin's Active Objects storage is usable by counting the rows of the AO_8BAD1B_BOOTSTRAP table through ActiveObjects.count. A count that returns (any number) means ready. A failure whose root cause is an IllegalStateException means 'Active Objects not ready yet' (a warning 'ActiveObjects is not ready. Waiting...' is logged) and the check is retried; any other runtime exception is not retried and propagates to the caller of the wait unchanged.

Storage access in the plugin (the database provider and the storage lock) first waits on this component. The first wait retries the readiness check up to 20 times, pausing after each failed check 100, 100, 100, 100, 200, 200, 200, 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000, 2000, 3000, then 5000 ms seven times (about 45 s in all). If the DarkFeatures integer almworks.ao.timeout is set to T > 0 (seconds), the pauses follow the same sequence, repeating 5000 ms at the end, until they add up to at least T*1000 ms. Once a check succeeds, every later wait returns immediately without checking again. Concurrent waiters are serialised: one thread runs the checks and the others wait for its outcome.

If no check succeeds within the schedule, the wait throws StructureStoppedException for the plugin key com.almworks.jira.structure. On the first such failure only, unless the DarkFeatures boolean structure.ignoreFailedStartup is true, the component asks the plugin's lifecycle module to shut the plugin down (disable it) with a prominent multi-line message saying that <product> failed to start and was automatically disabled because the database service (Active Objects) was not ready in time; with structure.ignoreFailedStartup true it only logs a prominent error saying Active Objects was not ready in time and leaves the plugin enabled. The shutdown request is made at most once per lifecycle instance. No network contact happens.

After the wait has given up once, each later wait makes a single immediate readiness check (no pauses, no 'waiting' warning): if it fails, StructureStoppedException is thrown at once; if it succeeds, the failure is forgotten and the wait completes normally, after which all waits return immediately.

If the waiting thread is interrupted during a pause, its interrupt flag is set again and the wait gives up as when the schedule runs out (first-failure shutdown handling included, StructureStoppedException thrown). If the component has been stopped (plugin stop) before or during the wait, the next check attempt throws StructureStoppedException instead of checking.

Waiting on a thread whose name contains 'jira-bootstrap' (ignoring case) is treated as a programming error: with Java assertions enabled (as the tests run) the wait throws AssertionError before checking; with them disabled, it logs an error about possible delays during Jira startup and then waits normally.

Two JVM system properties make the readiness check fail on purpose for testing: structure.testing.forceAOFail=true makes every check fail as 'not ready' (so the wait eventually gives up); structure.testing.forceAODelay=S (seconds, default 0) makes checks fail as 'not ready' until S seconds have passed since the first check that reached the database. Both are read when the component is created and log a warning on each forced failure.

The jira-components module carries no behaviour of its own beyond the public JiraComponents type: it registers JiraComponents as a plugin component only so that its shared proxy cache is emptied when the plugin's components start and stop and whenever all plugin caches are cleared (it is one of the caching components that structure-cache-helper clears); clearing one user's caches does nothing to it. The getters' behaviour is as already specified for JiraComponents.

Asked to install a fake current HTTP request on the calling thread, the component (Jira 9) checks com.atlassian.jira.web.ExecutingHttpRequest.get(): if a request is already present it leaves it alone and reports false; otherwise it sets a fake request (with a null response) through ExecutingHttpRequest.set and reports true. Clearing always calls ExecutingHttpRequest.clear(), whether or not the current request was installed by this component.

The fake request is a javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest whose getRequestURI() returns the Jira base URL (as StructureUtil.getBaseUrl gives it, an absolute URL, empty if unknown) and getRequestURL() a StringBuffer of the same text, and whose getContextPath() asks the context-path supplier given at install time on every call. Everything else is empty: no headers (getHeader null, getDateHeader and getIntHeader -1, empty header enumerations), no parameters (null values, empty map), no cookies (null), no attributes (setAttribute ignored), no session (getSession() and getSession(true) return null), method, scheme, server name and remote data null, ports 0, content length -1, locale Locale.ROOT, dispatcher type REQUEST, not secure, no user; startAsync and getAsyncContext throw IllegalStateException.

Given a bridged HTTP request (from servlet-bridges), the component (Jira 9) creates com.atlassian.jira.plugin.webfragment.model.JiraHelper objects for evaluating web fragments: either new JiraHelper(request), or new JiraHelper(request, project, params) with the given Jira project (may be null) and context parameter map, where request is the original javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest behind the bridge.

If the request behind the bridge is not a javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest (or is null), creating the helper throws IllegalArgumentException with the message 'Expected javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest, got: ' followed by the actual object's class name, or 'null'.

When the i18n web resource's URL is built, the component adds the query parameter locale with the current user's locale from JiraAuthenticationContext.getLocale(), written as the language, then '-' and the country if the country is not blank, then '-' and the variant if both country and variant are not blank (en_US gives 'en-US', fr gives 'fr', a locale with a variant but no country gives just the language). If Jira reports no locale (null), no parameter is added.

Only resources whose location starts with 'i18n/' and ends with '_messages.js' (the widget-i18n resource i18n/structure_messages.js, for example) are replaced by a generated message bundle; for every other resource the component answers 'not mine' and the transformer passes the original resource through unchanged.

The message keys to include are selected by prefixes taken from the resource's parameter i18n.prefixes (a comma-separated list) when it is not blank; otherwise the default list is used, which is exactly: sw., s.w., st.widget., s.g., s.generic., s.cfd., st.search., s.iv., s.end-of-life., s.stats-offer., s.manage.perm, s.manage.edit.select, s.manage.favorites, s.upm., str.admin.config.permission, str.admin.dark, s.permissions., s.p, s.issueDetails., s.itemDetails., s.tpl.structure, str.admin.support.syncAuditLog., s.action, s.gantt, common.words., s.effector, str.admin.attrSensitivity., user.picker., userpicker., assignee.types., reporter.types., common.resolution., common.filters., s.tempo, s.ext.it.item., s.wp. (in this order).

The locale of the bundle comes from the request's locale query parameter: blank or missing gives Locale.US; otherwise the text is split at '-' into 1, 2 or 3 parts giving new Locale(language), new Locale(language, country) or new Locale(language, country, variant) ('de-DE' gives de_DE); 4 or more parts give Locale.US (logged at debug). Parts are not validated or normalised beyond what java.util.Locale does.

Each message text is written as a single-quoted JavaScript string literal: first every property-file style apostrophe ('' or \') becomes a single apostrophe; then ' becomes \', a backslash becomes \\, newline \n, carriage return \r, U+2028 and U+2029 become \u2028 and \u2029, and every other character outside printable ASCII (space to '~') becomes \u followed by 4 lowercase hex digits; finally any '</script' (any letter case) becomes '\u003c/script'. A double quote is left as is.

The generated resource has content type text/javascript, a last-modified time equal to the moment the component was created rounded down to a whole second, and the ETag '"' + L.toString() + '.' + Integer.toHexString(java.util.Arrays.hashCode(bytes)) + '"' where bytes is the UTF-8 content (for example "en_US.1a2b3c" in quotes).

When the bundle is served: if the JVM system property atlassian.disable.caches is 'true' it is always sent in full without validator headers. Otherwise the response gets Last-Modified and ETag headers and a 304 status with no body is sent when both hold: the request's If-Modified-Since is absent or not earlier than last-modified minus 1000 ms, and If-None-Match equals the ETag, is '*', or is a comma-separated list containing the ETag (entries trimmed). A missing If-None-Match always means the full bundle is sent with the content type set.

A bundle is generated once per (L.toString() + prefix-list text) and then reused unchanged, without limit or expiry, until all plugin caches are cleared (the component is a caching component); clearing one user's caches does not affect it. Message changes in Jira therefore show only after a global cache clear or restart.

Storing a state object returns a new numeric id: 1 for the first state after plugin start, then 2, 3, ..., never reused while the plugin runs. The state is owned by the user key of StructureAuth.getUser() at the time (null for anonymous) and its last-access time is set to now. Storing null throws NullPointerException. States live only in this node's memory: they are lost on restart and not visible on other cluster nodes.

A state is accessible to the current user when the user is a Jira administrator (StructurePluginHelper.isAdmin()) or when the current StructureAuth user key equals the owner's key; states created anonymously are therefore accessible to every anonymous caller and to administrators.

Reading state id with an expected class returns the stored object and refreshes its last-access time. It fails with the component's checked state error, message 'no state <id>', if no such state exists (also for a null id); 'permission denied to get state <id>' if it is not accessible to the current user; and 'invalid state <id>, expected <class>, stored <class>' if the object is not an instance of the expected class (subclasses are accepted). A failed read does not refresh the access time.

Listing states of a class returns, ordered by id ascending, every stored state accessible to the current user whose object is an instance of the class; when asked to touch, each returned state's last-access time is refreshed, otherwise times are left unchanged. Inaccessible states are silently left out.

Removing an unknown id does nothing; removing a state not accessible to the current user does nothing except log a warning; otherwise the state is removed. Touching refreshes the last-access time of an accessible state and silently does nothing for unknown or inaccessible ids. Neither throws.

The first time a state is stored, the component schedules a repeating system job with job-manager (initial delay 30 minutes, then every 30 minutes); this is attempted only once per plugin run, and if scheduling fails a warning is logged and it is never retried. Each run removes every state whose last access is more than 6 hours (21,600,000 ms) ago, or lies in the future (clock moved back). Expiry happens only in these runs: a state idle for more than 6 hours is still returned by reads until the next run removes it.

On a single server (Jira's ClusterInfo absent or not clustered), the component does nothing: sending a message sends nothing, listeners can be added and removed but are never called, and Jira's ClusterMessagingService is never used.

On Data Center, when the component starts it registers one message consumer for the channel 'Structure' with Jira's ClusterMessagingService.registerListener; when it stops it unregisters that consumer and forgets all listeners. Messages arriving before start or after stop are not delivered.
On Data Center, sending a text message calls ClusterMessagingService.sendRemote('Structure', message) with the text unchanged; the sending node does not deliver the message to its own listeners.

On Data Center, a message received on channel 'Structure' is handed to every listener currently added, in the order they were added (a listener added twice is called twice; removing it removes one occurrence). An exception or linkage error thrown by one listener is logged as a warning and the remaining listeners are still called. Messages on any other channel are ignored. Listeners may be added and removed concurrently with delivery.

Clearing all caches on this node asks Jira's PluginAccessor.getEnabledModulesByClass(CachingComponent.class) for every enabled module object implementing CachingComponent and calls clearCaches() on each; an exception or linkage error from one of them is ignored (debug log) and the rest are still cleared; finally an info message 'Cleared all <product> caches' is logged (with ' on node <id>' on Data Center). If the module lookup itself fails, nothing is cleared and a warning is logged. Nothing is thrown to the caller.

Clearing one user's caches on this node calls clearUserCaches(user) on every enabled CachingComponent module object found as for clearing all, ignoring individual failures, then logs 'Cleared <product> caches for user <user>'.

Cache clearing through this component has an effect only while the plugin is fully running: it becomes active when the plugin lifecycle has started all components and inactive again when the plugin begins to stop or Jira publishes ComponentManagerShutdownEvent. While inactive, every clear (local, user, or one triggered by a cluster message) finds no caching components and clears nothing.

Clearing all caches on all nodes first clears all caches on this node and then sends the cluster message 'clearAllStructureCaches' through cluster-messaging-service-wrapper. Clearing a user's caches on all nodes first does the local clear for the user with that key (nothing if the key is null or no Jira user has it), then sends 'clearUserStructureCaches:<userKey>'. The message is sent even if the local part throws; a failure to send is logged as an error and not thrown. On a single server only the local part happens.

A node receiving the cluster message 'clearAllStructureCaches' clears all caches locally; receiving 'clearUserStructureCaches:<key>' (everything after the first colon is the key, which may itself contain colons) looks the user up by key and clears that user's caches locally, doing nothing if no user has the key. The bare text 'clearUserStructureCaches' (no colon) and any message whose part before the first colon is not one of these names are ignored by this component. The receiving node does not send anything further.

The component knows exactly seven named date styles, listed in this order: date-short, date-long, date-full, datetime-short, datetime-long, jira-date, jira-datetime. date-short, date-long and date-full format like java.text.DateFormat.getDateInstance with SHORT, LONG and FULL; datetime-short and datetime-long like DateFormat.getDateTimeInstance with SHORT/SHORT and LONG/LONG; all five use the current user's locale and the time zone Jira's TimeZoneManager.getTimeZoneforUser gives for StructureAuth.getUser(). jira-date and jira-datetime use Jira's DateTimeFormatterFactory.formatter().forUser(StructureAuth.getUser()) with DateTimeStyle.DATE and DateTimeStyle.COMPLETE. Formats are built fresh on each request, so changes of the user's locale or zone apply at once.
Asking for a date format by a style name that is not one of the seven (including null or empty) gives the date-short format. The short date-time format is the same as datetime-short.

A style is reported as including the time of day exactly when it is one of the seven known styles and its name contains 'time': true for datetime-short, datetime-long and jira-datetime; false for date-short, date-long, date-full, jira-date and for any unknown name.

Listing the styles gives all seven style names in the order above, each with a sample text formatting the given date in that style for the current user; when no sample date is given (null), every sample is null.

The current user's locale is the locale of the I18nHelper Jira's I18nHelper.BeanFactory gives for StructureAuth.getUser(); for an anonymous user, or if that locale is null, Jira's default locale (as StructureUtil.getJiraDefaultLocale reports it, remembered after the first lookup) is used.

Formatting a duration of N milliseconds as Jira time-tracking text: if |N| is below 60000 (under a minute, zero included) the result is '0m'; otherwise it is Jira's JiraDurationUtils.getShortFormattedDuration of |N|/1000 seconds (integer division), in the current user's locale for the user-specific variant and with Jira's default (no locale argument) for the plain variant, prefixed by '-' when N is negative (e.g. -7200000 gives '-2h' with standard settings).

Formatting a duration of N milliseconds as calendar time uses com.atlassian.core.util.DateUtils.getDurationString (calendar units: 1 day = 24 hours, 1 week = 7 days) of |N|/1000 seconds, with |N| below 60000 treated as 0, and prefixes '-' when N is at most -60000.

Parsing Jira time-tracking text: null or empty text gives null; otherwise the result is exactly what Jira's JiraDurationUtils.parseDuration(text, locale) returns for the StructureAuth user's locale (seconds, not converted to milliseconds), and its InvalidDurationException propagates. Parsing with explicit hours per day and days per week returns com.atlassian.core.util.DateUtils.getDuration(text, hoursPerDay, daysPerWeek) multiplied by 1000 (milliseconds); parsing as calendar time returns DateUtils.getDuration(text) multiplied by 1000. Invalid text gives com.atlassian.core.util.InvalidDurationException.
On Jira 9 the component reports whether attachments are enabled by returning Jira's AttachmentManager.attachmentsEnabled() as is, asked anew on every call; an exception from Jira propagates.

The component holds Jira's com.atlassian.jira.datetime.DateTimeFormatter. For a user (null allowed, Jira then formats for anonymous) it returns formatter.forUser(user); for a locale it returns formatter.withSystemZone().withLocale(locale), i.e. Jira's default time zone with that locale. If Jira's call returns null, the unmodified injected formatter is returned instead.

The date-formatting function it builds for a context key K and a 'user-based' flag formats a Unix timestamp in milliseconds as a date (DateTimeStyle.DATE): user-based means in the zone and locale of the AttributeContext's user (forUser(context.getUser())), otherwise in Jira's system zone with the context's locale. The formatter is built once per AttributeContext and stored in it with AttributeContext.putObject under K, so later calls in the same context reuse it; a different context builds its own.

Correcting a date-only field value for display takes the timestamp's calendar date in the JVM default time zone and returns the start of that same date (00:00) in the AttributeContext's time zone (context.getTimeZone()), in epoch milliseconds; e.g. with JVM zone UTC and context zone Europe/Berlin, 2024-03-10T00:00Z gives 2024-03-09T23:00Z. The conversion is set up once per context, stored under the context object key 'DateFieldTimestampCorrectionFunction', and reused within that context.

The Portfolio date correction converts a timestamp from time zone 'from' to time zone 'to' the same way (calendar date in 'from', start of that date in 'to'). The conversion is stored in the AttributeContext under the key 'PortfolioTimestampCorrectionFunction' the first time it is used in a context, and later calls in the same context reuse that first conversion even when they pass different 'from' or 'to' zones (as the original does).

The date helpers convert: a timestamp (or java.util.Date) to the java.time.LocalDate it falls on in a given zone (a zone given as text is resolved with ZoneId.of, so an unknown id throws java.time.DateTimeException); a LocalDate to the epoch milliseconds of its start of day in the JVM default zone; a Date to the LocalDateTime in a given zone; and they offer the same 'calendar date in source zone, start of day in target zone' conversion from UTC to a zone and from a zone to the JVM default zone. Daylight-saving gaps follow java.time's atStartOfDay rules.

Rendering wiki markup to HTML uses Jira's renderer for type 'atlassian-wiki-renderer' from RendererManager.getRendererForType, looked up once on first use and then reused (a null answer is remembered too). The text is rendered with render(text, null), i.e. without an issue context. Null text gives the empty string without asking Jira. If Jira has no such renderer, the text is returned HTML-escaped (as com.opensymphony.util.TextUtils.htmlEncode does) instead of rendered.

Rendering as plain text returns the text HTML-escaped as com.opensymphony.util.TextUtils.htmlEncode does (null gives the empty string); the variant with line breaks additionally turns line breaks into HTML break tags as TextUtils.br does. Neither uses Jira's renderer.

On Jira 9 the component builds static resource URLs through Jira's com.atlassian.plugin.webresource.WebResourceUrlProvider: the URL of a plugin resource given by module complete key (or module descriptor) and resource name, the static resource prefix with or without a resource counter. The requested URL mode (absolute, relative or automatic) is passed as the platform com.atlassian.plugin.webresource.UrlMode of the same name (ABSOLUTE, RELATIVE, AUTO). Results are Jira's, unchanged.

On Jira 9 the component forwards to Jira's JiraWebResourceManager: requiring a web resource by complete module key (requireResource), requiring all resources of a context (requireResourcesForContext), returning the HTML tags of the resources required so far as given by getRequiredResources(UrlMode.AUTO), and putting a page metadata key and value (putMetadata), returning Jira's boolean result.

On Jira 9 (javax servlet API) the component wraps an object as a bridged request only if it is a javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest, and as a bridged response only if it is a javax.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse; anything else, including null, throws IllegalArgumentException ('request must be an instance of javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest' / 'response must be an instance of javax.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse'). Each call creates a new wrapper.

A bridged request answers header, date header, server name and port, context path, scheme, query string, method and parameter by asking the wrapped request directly, and gives back the wrapped request itself as the original. Cookies are returned as a list of name/value pairs in the request's order, an empty list when the request has no cookies (null). Asking for the session with or without creation returns a bridged session around the request's HttpSession, or null when there is none; a bridged session reads and writes session attributes directly.

A bridged response forwards reading header values by name, setting and adding headers, setting date headers, status, content type, character encoding and buffer size, reset, and access to the output stream and writer directly to the wrapped javax response; IOExceptions from the stream and writer propagate.

On Jira 9 the component forwards to Jira's com.atlassian.jira.util.velocity.VelocityRequestContextFactory: getting the current Jira Velocity request context (getJiraVelocityRequestContext), setting it from a given context, setting it from a base URL plus a bridged request, and clearing it; caching a request context from a base URL plus a bridged request uses Jira's static DefaultVelocityRequestContextFactory.cacheVelocityRequestContext.

Setting or caching the context from a bridged request whose original request is not a javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest (or is null) throws IllegalArgumentException with message 'Expected javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest, got: ' followed by the class name of the bridge object rather than of the request (as the original does); Jira is not called.

On Jira 9 the component looks up Jira's com.atlassian.jira.web.HttpServletVariables through ComponentAccessor.getComponent on every call and returns its current HTTP request, or response, wrapped by servlet-bridges. Outside an HTTP request the result depends on Jira: if Jira's call throws, the exception propagates; if it returns null, wrapping fails with IllegalArgumentException.

On Jira 9 the component returns the current web action's request and response, as webwork's action context reports them (its static getRequest and getResponse), wrapped by servlet-bridges, asked anew on every call. When no action is running and webwork reports null, wrapping fails with IllegalArgumentException.

On Jira 9 the component prints a java.util.Calendar as an XML Schema dateTime string and parses such a string back into a Calendar exactly as javax.xml.bind.DatatypeConverter.printDateTime and parseDateTime do (e.g. 2024-05-06T07:08:09.123+02:00; the zone of the calendar is kept). Text that is not a valid lexical xsd:dateTime makes parsing throw IllegalArgumentException.

`issue-constant-icon-cache` keeps the HTML it rendered in memory, keyed per input (see the key claim), with no size limit. The whole cache is emptied (not entry by entry) on first use and on the first lookup made more than the time-to-live after the last emptying; the time-to-live is read once at construction from the dark feature `structure.iconConstantCache.ttl` in seconds, default 300 (5 minutes); the same property governs all three icon caches. Within that window a repeated lookup for the same key returns the stored HTML without asking Jira again, even if the underlying icon, name or avatar changed.

`issue-constant-icon-cache` is a `CachingComponent`: `clearCaches()`, `clearUserCaches(user)` and `clearUserCaches(userKey)` each empty the whole cache (not just one user's entries) and restart the time-to-live window, so the next lookup renders anew.

`user-icon-cache` keeps the HTML it rendered in memory, keyed per input (see the key claim), with no size limit. The whole cache is emptied (not entry by entry) on first use and on the first lookup made more than the time-to-live after the last emptying; the time-to-live is read once at construction from the dark feature `structure.iconConstantCache.ttl` in seconds, default 300 (5 minutes); the same property governs all three icon caches. Within that window a repeated lookup for the same key returns the stored HTML without asking Jira again, even if the underlying icon, name or avatar changed.

`user-icon-cache` is a `CachingComponent`: `clearCaches()`, `clearUserCaches(user)` and `clearUserCaches(userKey)` each empty the whole cache (not just one user's entries) and restart the time-to-live window, so the next lookup renders anew.

`user-printable-icon-cache` keeps the HTML it rendered in memory, keyed per input (see the key claim), with no size limit. The whole cache is emptied (not entry by entry) on first use and on the first lookup made more than the time-to-live after the last emptying; the time-to-live is read once at construction from the dark feature `structure.iconConstantCache.ttl` in seconds, default 300 (5 minutes); the same property governs all three icon caches. Within that window a repeated lookup for the same key returns the stored HTML without asking Jira again, even if the underlying icon, name or avatar changed.

`user-printable-icon-cache` is a `CachingComponent`: `clearCaches()`, `clearUserCaches(user)` and `clearUserCaches(userKey)` each empty the whole cache (not just one user's entries) and restart the time-to-live window, so the next lookup renders anew.

For a Jira `IssueConstant` (issue type, priority, status, resolution) `issue-constant-icon-cache` returns ``, where NAME is the constant's name translated with the `AttributeContext`'s i18n helper (`getNameTranslation`) and URL the absolute icon URL (see the URL claim); both are HTML-escaped with Jira's `TextUtils.htmlEncode`.

The icon URL is the constant's `getIconUrl()` trimmed: when it starts with `http://` or `https://` it is used as is, otherwise it is prefixed with Jira's base URL from SAL `ApplicationProperties.getBaseUrl()` (trimmed; empty when the SAL service is missing), with no slash added between them.
`issue-constant-icon-cache` returns the empty string (and caches it) for a null constant, and for a constant whose icon URL is null, blank or exactly `/`.

Entries of `issue-constant-icon-cache` are keyed by the constant's Java class simple name, its id and the `AttributeContext`'s locale (`<SimpleName>:<id>:<locale>`), so the same constant is rendered separately per locale, and an issue type and a priority with the same id do not collide. A null constant has key `""`. The base URL is not part of the key.

For a user, `user-icon-cache` asks SAL `UserManager.getUserProfile(username)` and takes `getProfilePictureUri(w, h)` with w = h = the pixel size of Jira's small avatar (`Avatar.Size.SMALL`, 24 on Jira 9). It returns ``, where NAME is the HTML-escaped `ApplicationUser.getName()` and AVATAR the profile picture URI as given (not escaped). HTML escaping uses Jira's `TextUtils.htmlEncode`.

For a null user, or a user for whom SAL returns no profile, `user-icon-cache` returns ``, where BASE is the `AttributeContext`'s base URL and ID Jira's anonymous avatar id from `AvatarManager.getAnonymousAvatarId()` (looked up once per `AttributeContext` and kept in it).
Entries of `user-icon-cache` are keyed by the user's key only (not by locale or base URL); a null user has key `""`. A user without a profile is cached under its own key with the anonymous HTML.

For a user, `user-printable-icon-cache` asks SAL `UserManager.getUserProfile(username)` and takes `getProfilePictureUri(w, h)` with w = h = the pixel size of Jira's small avatar (`Avatar.Size.SMALL`, 24 on Jira 9). It returns ``, where USERNAME is the HTML-escaped `getUsername()`, DISPLAY the HTML-escaped `getDisplayName()` and AVATAR the profile picture URI as given (not escaped). HTML escaping uses Jira's `TextUtils.htmlEncode`.

For a null user, or a user for whom SAL returns no profile, `user-printable-icon-cache` returns ``, where BASE is the `AttributeContext`'s base URL and ID Jira's anonymous avatar id from `AvatarManager.getAnonymousAvatarId()` (looked up once per `AttributeContext` and kept in it).

Entries of `user-printable-icon-cache` are keyed by the user's key only (not by locale or base URL); a null user has key `""`. A user without a profile is cached under its own key with the anonymous HTML.
`user-field-renderer` returns null for a null user and for a user for whom SAL `UserManager.getUserProfile(username)` returns no profile.

For a user with a SAL profile, `user-field-renderer` renders the Velocity template `/templates/structure/field/user.vm` (its own resource) with Jira's `VelocityTemplatingEngine` as HTML (`asHtml()`), with Jira's default Velocity parameters for the current user (from `VelocityRequestContextFactory.getDefaultVelocityParams` and the plugin's authentication context) plus: `url` = Jira base URL + the profile's `getProfilePageUri()`, `username` = profile user name, `displayName` = profile full name, `avatarUrl` = the profile's `getProfilePictureUri()` (default size), `view` = the requested view mode or `""` when null. The extra parameters win over the defaults.

The rendered HTML depends on the view mode. `avatar`: a link `` holding only the extra-small avatar (``). `name`: the same link holding only the display name as text. Any other value (including none): the same link holding the avatar followed by `DISPLAYNAME`. Whether values are HTML-escaped depends on Jira's Velocity escaping at run time.

`item-property-editors` gives an editor for the item property name `notes` (the built-in default note; never archived) and for `dc_note_<n>` when `note-manager` knows a note with that id (archived or not, remembering whether it is archived at lookup time). For any other name, or a `dc_note_` name with no stored note, it gives no editor (null), so the property cannot be edited through the item update REST call.

Editing through an editor stores the value as the item property (structure id, item, property name = the note id `notes` / `dc_note_<n>`) via the plugin's per-structure item property store (`AO_8BAD1B_ITEM_PROPERTY`; a blank value deletes the row there). Errors are not thrown: they are added as error messages to the given Jira `ErrorCollection` and nothing is stored.

An edit is refused, with exactly one error message and nothing stored, in this order: the note is archived (text of `s.itemproperty.notes.edit.archived.unavailable`, English `Cannot edit or add values for archived notes.`); the item does not resolve through `ItemResolver.resolveItem(item, Object.class)` (`s.itemproperty.notes.edit.unavailable` with the item description, `Cannot edit notes for an unavailable item: {0}.`); the `ForestSpec` has no structure id or id 0 (`s.itemproperty.notes.edit.no.structure`, `Notes can be edited only for a particular structure.`); the current user lacks EDIT on the structure per `StructureManager.isAccessible(id, EDIT)` (`s.item.edit.error.no-edit-perm` with the structure id, `No "Edit" permission for structure {0}.`). The note's own permission scheme is not consulted.

When the item property store rejects the write with `IllegalArgumentException` (for example a property key it cannot encode) or fails with a storage error, the editor adds the error message `s.itemproperty.notes.edit.failed` (`Failed to update notes.`) and returns normally.

`note-searcher` searches the built-in default note (id `notes`, name = text of `s.w.notes.note.default`, English `Notes (Default)`) and every non-archived stored note. A note matches when the term is the empty string, or when the term, trimmed, occurs anywhere in the note's name as literal text (no wildcards or regex), ignoring case (Unicode-aware).

A term made only of whitespace matches no note at all (the empty-term rule applies only to the untrimmed empty string), so the result has no groups and no more-results flag (as the original does). A null term throws `NullPointerException`.

Results come as groups in this order, each present only when non-empty: (1) an untitled group with just the default note, if it matches; (2) the group titled `s.w.notes.note.search.used-notes` (`Used in structure`): matching stored notes that have at least one value in the given structure, only when the current user can VIEW that structure (`StructureManager.isAccessible`); (3) the group titled `s.w.notes.note.search.other-notes` (`Other notes`), computed only while the limit is not exceeded: matching notes not yet listed that have a value in any structure the current user can VIEW, plus the remaining matching notes whose permission scheme gives the current user view access (per `permission-scheme-manager`). Each note appears in at most one group.

Notes listed because they have values in the given structure or in another structure the user can view are listed regardless of the note's own permission scheme; only notes with no values in a viewable structure need the scheme's view permission.
Within groups 2 and 3, notes are sorted by name with plain case-sensitive `String` order, then by id as a string (so `dc_note_10` comes before `dc_note_9`).

With a null limit every group is complete and the more-results flag is false. With limit L, groups are taken in order while the remaining count is positive; a group is cut to the remaining count, and after each group the remaining count drops by the group's full size. A group met when the remaining count is 0 is left out. The more-results flag (REST `hasMore`) is true when the remaining count went below 0, i.e. more matching notes were found than L. Example: L = 2 with the default note and 3 used notes gives the default note, the first used note, and `hasMore` true; group 3 is not computed.
Limit 0 gives no groups; `hasMore` is true when at least one note matches, false when none does. A negative limit gives no groups and `hasMore` true, even when no note matches at all.

`saved-column-manager` knows exactly two saved-column sources, listed in this order: `bundled` (`bundled-column-source`) then `stored` (`stored-column-source`). Looking a source up by id gives that source for `bundled` or `stored`, and nothing (null) for any other id; REST calls on another source id fail as not found.

A view column refers to a saved column through its parameter `savedColumn`, whose text must be `[modified/]<sourceId>/<columnId>` with a decimal column id; the source id is everything between the optional `modified/` prefix and the last `/`. A value of another shape makes adjusting the view specification throw `IllegalArgumentException` (`Column id does not match the declared format: ...`). Columns without the parameter are left untouched, as are columns whose source id is unknown.

When a view specification is adjusted for a user, each column with an unmodified reference `<source>/<id>` is looked up in its source ignoring permissions: if the saved column no longer exists the column is removed from the specification; otherwise the column's key becomes the saved column's type and its parameters are replaced by the saved column's parameters, plus `savedColumn` = `<source>/<id>` when the user may read the saved column, without it when not. The column's csid and name are kept; column order and other columns are unchanged.

A column with a `modified/<source>/<id>` reference keeps its own key and parameters. If the user may not read that saved column (including when it no longer exists), the `savedColumn` parameter is removed from the column; otherwise the column is left as it is.

Every `StructureView` returned by `view-manager` reports its specification adjusted this way, with the security override and user key that were current when the view object was obtained; the stored view data in `AO_8BAD1B_VIEW` is not changed by it.

`stored-column-source` has source id `stored` and two lists in this order: `global` (name = text of `s.w.saved-column.list.global`, English `Global`) with every global saved column (`AO_8BAD1B_SAVED_COLUMN` rows with `C_OWNER` NULL), and `user` (`s.w.saved-column.list.user`, `My Columns`) with the current user's own columns. Anonymous users get an empty `user` list; with security overridden the `user` list holds every user's columns (read uncached). Each saved column's list key is `global` without owner and `user` with one.

The `global` list reports create-supported when security is overridden or `StructurePluginHelper.isManageGlobalSavedColumnsAllowed(current user)` is true; the `user` list when the user is not anonymous (or security is overridden).

Listing, reading, creating, updating, moving and deleting stored columns first require, unless security is overridden, that `StructurePluginHelper.isStructureAvailableToUser(current user)` is true (the user found by key; null for anonymous); otherwise they throw `StructureException` `STRUCTURE_PLUGIN_ACCESS_DENIED`. The readable/editable/movable checks do not make this check.
Reading one stored column by id returns it when it exists and is global, or is owned by the current user, or security is overridden; another user's column and a missing id give null (not an error).

Creating into list `user` stores a personal column owned by the current user (anonymous: `StructureException` `SAVED_COLUMN_MANAGEMENT_DENIED`, even with security overridden but no user); into `global` stores a column with no owner and requires security override or the manage-global-saved-columns permission (`SAVED_COLUMN_MANAGEMENT_DENIED` otherwise); any other list key throws `IllegalArgumentException` (`List is not supported: <key>`). Type and parameters are not validated here; the name is mandatory, and a blank one or one over 190 characters is refused when the input is read. The new row goes into `AO_8BAD1B_SAVED_COLUMN` (via `saved-column-io`).

Updating or deleting a stored column: a missing id throws `StructureException` `SAVED_COLUMN_NOT_EXISTS_OR_NOT_ACCESSIBLE`. Unless security is overridden: a global column requires the manage-global-saved-columns permission (`SAVED_COLUMN_MANAGEMENT_DENIED`); a personal column requires a logged-in user (`SAVED_COLUMN_MANAGEMENT_DENIED` for anonymous) who is its owner (`SAVED_COLUMN_NOT_EXISTS_OR_NOT_ACCESSIBLE` for another user's column). Nothing is changed when a check fails.

A stored column can be moved only to list `global`: the move is allowed when the column exists, has an owner, the owner is the current user (or security is overridden) and the user may manage global saved columns (or security is overridden). The move clears `C_OWNER`, making the column global. A refused move throws `StructureException` `SAVED_COLUMN_MANAGEMENT_DENIED`; there is no way back to `user`.

When asked whether a move is possible with an error collection, a refused move adds one general error: target list not `global`, or column owned by someone else, or no manage-global permission: `s.w.saved-column.error.user-cannot-move` with the target list key (`User cannot move column to {0}`); missing column: `s.w.saved-column.error.not-found.edit` (`Unable to edit the saved column because it has been deleted`); column already global: `s.w.saved-column.error.column-moved-to-global` (`Cannot edit saved column because it has been moved to global`).

A stored column is readable when it exists and (security overridden, or it is global, or the current user owns it). It is editable when it exists and (security overridden, or the current user owns it, or it is global and the user may manage global saved columns). Missing columns are neither. This editable answer is what REST reports as `editable`.

For backup, the extra data of a stored column is `{"owner": <user key>}` for a personal column and null for a global or missing one. Restoring from backup: creating from backup stores a personal column for the given `owner` (any value turned to text) or a global column when there is no owner; restoring with an explicit id recreates the row with that id and owner. All three need security overridden, otherwise `StructureException` `INVALID_PARAMETER` (`This operation is only available in sudo context`).

The replacement does no licence checking: creating, updating, moving and deleting stored saved columns are never refused or made read-only on licence grounds (SPEC.md §1.1, §1.8), although the REST descriptions mention a licence read-only mode.

`bundled-column-source` has source id `bundled` and one list with key `bundled`, named by the text of `s.w.saved-column.list.bundled` (English `Bundled`), never create-supported. Every bundled column is readable by anyone (no permission check, also for anonymous users), never editable or movable, and its list key is `bundled`. Creating, updating, moving or deleting a bundled column throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Reading by an unknown id gives null.

Every bundled column has type `formula`; its name and description are i18n texts looked up with the plugin helper's i18n (current user's locale) each time they are read. Its parameters hold `formula` (the expression text), usually `variables` (a map from variable name to an attribute spec `{"id": <attribute id>, "format": <value format id>}`, plus `params` where noted) and usually `displayFormat`. Unless stated, a bundled column is neither featured nor should-open-configurator.

The bundled columns are built on first use and then kept for the life of the component. Which of them exist and how they look (see the story points and sprint claims) is decided once, from the fields visible to the user who triggered that first use.

The bundled list holds, in this order: 1 BugFix % (Time), 2 BugFix % (Count), WSJF (Basic) as 3 (story points field found) or 4 (not found), 5 WSJF (Tempo), 6 WSJF (SAFe), 7 Total Work Ratio (Points) (only with a story points field), 8 Total Work Ratio (Time), 9 Total Underestimation, 10 Time to Resolve, 11 Due In, 12 Time Since Last Update, 13 Assignee Cost, 14 Unresolved Blockers, 15 Item Health, 16 Tasks Since Sprint Started (only when a Sprint field exists), 17 Time Flagged. The numbers are the column ids (REST `bundled/<id>`).

The story points field is the first field, in the order Jira's `FieldManager.getAvailableNavigableFields(current user)` returns them, whose name, lower-cased with `Locale.US` and stripped of every character that is not a letter or digit, equals `storypoints` (so `Story Points`, `Story-points`, `story_points` all match). Its variable spec is the field turned into an attribute spec with format `number`: a custom field `customfield_<n>` gives `{"id": "customfield", "format": "number", "params": {"fieldId": <n>}}`, a system field `{"id": <field id>, "format": "number"}`.

The Sprint field is the custom field that `gh-integration` reports as Jira Software's Sprint field; none when it reports none. Its variable spec is `{"id": "customfield", "format": "text", "params": {"fieldId": <n>}}`.

Bundled column 1, name key `s.w.formula.preset.bugfixPercent.time` (English `BugFix % (Time)`, description key with `.description`: `Displays percent of time spent on fixing bugs`), is featured. Variables: `type` = `issuetype` (text), `timespent` = `timespent` (duration), `estimate` = `timeestimate` (duration). Formula: total = sum over the sub-tree (including the row) of time spent + remaining estimate; when total > 0, the same sum over rows whose type is `bug`, divided by total (no value otherwise). Display format `{"type": "percentage", "rounding": 0}`.

Bundled column 2, `s.w.formula.preset.bugfixPercent.count` (`BugFix % (Count)`, `Displays percent of all sub-issues that are bugs`). Variables: `type` = `issuetype` (text), `itemtype` = `itemtype` (text). Formula: total = sum over the sub-tree of 1 for each row whose item type is `issue`; when total > 0, the count of rows of type `bug` divided by total, else 0. Display format percentage, rounding 0.

WSJF (Basic), `s.w.formula.preset.wsjf` (`WSJF (Basic)`, `Weighted Shortest Job First, a measurement of issues benefit/cost ratio`), is featured; id 3 when a story points field exists, else id 4. Variables: `priority` = `priority` (text), `votes` = `votes` (number), `duedate` = `duedate` (time), `remainingestimate` = `timeestimate` (duration), `resolution` = `resolution` (text), `itemtype` = `itemtype` (text), `watches` = `watches` (number), and for id 3 also `storypoints` = the story points spec. Formula, only for unresolved rows of item type `issue`: priority value (Highest 160, High 80, Medium 40, Low 20, Lowest 10, otherwise 40) × interest (1 + votes + watches / 10) × due factor (1.5 with a due date, else 1) × 100, divided by 1 + cost. Id 3 cost: (10 + calendar hours of the remaining estimate / 4 when set) + (10 + story points / 4 when set) + (20 when neither is set). Id 4 cost: 10 + calendar hours of the remaining estimate / 4 when set, else 20. Display format `{"type": "number", "rounding": 0}`.

Bundled column 5, `s.w.formula.preset.wsjf.alm` (`WSJF (Tempo)`, `Weighted Shortest Job First metric, according to categories suggested by Tempo`), should open the configurator. Only variable: `itemtype` = `itemtype` (text); the others (`Benefit`, `Pain`, `Marketability`, `Impact`, `Cost`, `Risk`, `Clarity`) are left for the user to bind. Formula, for rows of item type `issue`: 100 × Bang / Buck, where Bang = (1 + benefit + pain + marketing) × impact and Buck = 1 + cost × risk × clarity, with the mappings benefit Low 1 / Medium 2 / High 5 / else 0; pain Low 1 / Medium 3 / High 6 / else 0; marketing (Marketability) Medium 1 / High 4 / else 0; impact Low 0.8 / Medium 1.2 / High 2 / else 1; cost Low 1 / Medium 1.5 / High 3 / else 2; risk Low 1 / Medium 1.5 / High 3 / else 2; clarity Medium 1 / High 0.9 / else 1.5. Display format number, rounding 0.

Bundled column 6, `s.w.formula.preset.wsjf.safe` (`WSJF (SAFe)`, `Weighted Shortest Job First metric, as suggested by Scaled Agile, Inc`), should open the configurator and has no `variables` parameter. Its formula is a template with placeholders `Size_Field_Or_Expression`, `Value_Field_Or_Expression`, `Criticality_Field_Or_Expression`, `RiskReduction_Field_Or_Expression`, `Opportunity_Field_Or_Expression` for job size, user-business value, time criticality, risk reduction and opportunity enablement; cost of delay = value + criticality + (risk reduction or, if that is empty, opportunity enablement); result, when job size > 0: cost of delay / job size. Display format `{"type": "number", "rounding": 2}`.

Bundled column 7 (only with a story points field), `s.w.formula.preset.wr.points` (`Total Work Ratio (Points)`). Variables: `storypoints` = the story points spec, `resolution` = `resolution` (text). Formula: when the sum of story points over the sub-tree is > 0, the sum of story points of resolved rows divided by it. Display format `{"type": "percentage", "rounding": 1}`.

Bundled column 8, `s.w.formula.preset.wr.time` (`Total Work Ratio (Time)`). Variables: `timespent` = `timespent` (duration), `estimate` = `timeestimate` (duration). Formula: spent = sum of time spent over the sub-tree, remaining = sum of remaining estimate; when spent + remaining > 0, spent / (spent + remaining). Display format percentage, rounding 1.

Bundled column 9, `s.w.formula.preset.time.underestimation` (`Total Underestimation`). Variables: `timespent` = `timespent`, `remaining` = `timeestimate`, `original_estimate` = `timeoriginalestimate` (all duration). Formula: original = sum of original estimates over the sub-tree; when original > 0, (sum of time spent + remaining over the sub-tree − original) / original. Display format percentage, rounding 1.

Bundled columns 10–12 all use display format `{"type": "duration", "workTime": false}`. 10 `s.w.formula.preset.time.ttr` (`Time to Resolve`): variables `resolved` = `resolutiondate` (time), `created` = `created` (time); when resolved is set, resolved − created. 11 `s.w.formula.preset.time.duein` (`Due In`): variable `duedate` = `duedate` (time); when the due date is set, due date − now if positive, otherwise the text `Overdue`. 12 `s.w.formula.preset.time.tslu` (`Time Since Last Update`): variable `updated` = `updated` (time); when set, now − updated.

Bundled column 13, `s.w.formula.preset.time.cost-assignee` (`Σ Assignee Cost`). Variables: `assignee` = `assignee` (text), `remainingestimate` = `timeestimate` (duration), `timespent` = `timespent` (duration), `rate` = attribute `user-property` (text) with params `{"userKey": {"id": "assignee", "format": "text"}, "propertyName": "Hourly Rate"}`. Formula: when the row has an assignee and a rate and remaining + spent > 0, rate × calendar hours of (remaining + spent). Other parameters: `aggregate` = `sum`, `distinct` = true, `forestSpec` = `displayed`; no display format.

Bundled column 14, `s.w.formula.preset.unresolved-blockers` (`Unresolved Blockers`). Variables: `issuelinks` = `issuelinkobjects` (any), `this` = `item` (any). Formula: from the row's issue links, those of link type `blocks` whose destination is this item and whose source is unresolved, giving their source issues (an array). No display format.

Bundled column 15, `s.w.formula.preset.item-health` (`Item Health`). Variable `progress` = attribute `progress` (number) with params `{"basedOn": "timetracking", "includeSelf": true, "resolvedComplete": true}`. Formula: a wiki-markup panel showing a status by progress: > 0.7 `Great` (background `59B161`, Structure icon `shine`, padding 12); > 0.3 `OK` (`FFAF00`, `partly-cloudy`, 21); otherwise `At Risk` (`EF4B59`, `thunderbolt`, 7). Each panel is borderless with that background colour, the 20×20 icon, a spacer image of the padding width, the status in bold white, and another spacer (icons by URL from the Structure icon set, including `spacer`). Display format `{"type": "wiki"}`.

Bundled column 16 (only when a Sprint field exists), `s.w.formula.preset.tasks-since-sprint` (`Tasks Since Sprint Started`). Variables: `history` = `history` (any), `sprint` = the Sprint field spec. Formula: over the sub-tree, counts rows whose latest change of field `sprint` happened after the start date of the latest of the row's sprints. Display format number, rounding 0.

Bundled column 17, `s.w.formula.preset.time-flagged` (`Time Flagged`). Variable `history` = `history` (any). Formula: from the change history of field `flagged`, takes the times it was set to `Impediment` and the times it was cleared (set to empty); when it was flagged at least once, the sum over each flag-on time of (the matching clear time by position, or now when there is none) minus the flag-on time. Display format duration, workTime false.

`extension-service` keeps, for each extension module type, the modules of that type that are enabled in Jira (from any plugin, via `PluginAccessor.getEnabledModuleDescriptorsByClass`): `structure-item-type` (item types), the generator types `structure-inserter`, `structure-extender`, `structure-grouper`, `structure-filter`, `structure-sorter` (one generator catalogue), `structure-synchronizer`, `structure-effector`, `structure-effect-provider`, `structure-attribute-loader-provider`, `structure-export-renderer-provider`, `structure-query-constraint`, `structure-core-extension`, `structure-performance-log-provider`, `structure-query-skeleton-factory`, `structure-backup-provider`, `structure-calendar-provider` and `structure-integration-details-provider`. With no enabled module of a type the corresponding catalogue is empty.

Each catalogue is built on first request and reused until a module of that type is enabled or disabled (Atlassian `PluginModuleEnabledEvent` / `PluginModuleDisabledEvent`, listened to while started); then it is rebuilt on the next request. Each such change also asks for all plugin caches to be cleared, throttled to at most once per `structure.clear.cache.min.interval` ms (dark feature, default 1000): every enabled `CachingComponent` module gets `clearCaches()`.

On start the component registers for plugin events, drops all catalogues and clears all plugin caches at once (every enabled `CachingComponent`). Before start, requests are served (built from Jira but not refreshed by events). After stop it unregisters, drops all catalogues, ignores module events and answers every request with the empty catalogue; it cannot be started again after a stop.

A module whose `getModule()` throws (any `Exception` or `LinkageError`) or returns an object of the wrong type is left out of its catalogue with a warning; it does not fail the catalogue or the caller.

Attribute loader providers, synchronizers and query constraints (module types with an order) are taken in ascending order using Jira's module descriptor comparator; other types are taken in the order Jira returns them. Attribute loader providers and synchronizers read the order from the `order` attribute (default 0); query constraints read it from an `<order>` child element (default `Integer.MAX_VALUE`).

Item types, generators, synchronizers, effectors and effect providers are looked up by the module's complete key (`<plugin key>:<module key>`, for example `com.almworks.jira.structure:type-issue`); an unknown key gives null (the item type for a null `ItemIdentity` is null). Core extensions, query skeleton factories and calendar providers are maps by complete key; when two modules share a key, the later one wins with a warning. Attribute loader providers and performance log providers are plain lists.

Resolving a generator by complete key throws `StructureException` `UNAVAILABLE_MODULE` (`Generator module <key> is not found`) when no enabled generator module has that key, and `UNAVAILABLE_MODULE` (`Generator module <key> failed to resolve`) when its module object cannot be obtained as a `StructureGenerator`; otherwise it gives the generator bound to the given parameters and owning structure. The generator catalogue also tells whether a key is present and lists all generator modules.
